# 2 Baruch Chapter 21 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

This log records all verses in 2 Baruch Chapter 21 where the three translators (EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA) significantly diverged in their renderings, along with SOPHIA's resolution and reasoning.

---

## 21:6 — "upheld / sustained / kept alive"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "who-sustained the-living-ones by-your-word" | Preserves Syriac verbal stem meaning "to uphold/sustain" |
| LOGOS | "who upheld the living by your word" | Standard formal rendering |
| PNEUMA | "You have sustained the living by your word" | Shifts to second-person direct address for rhetorical flow |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS "upheld." The Syriac verb conveys sustaining/upholding in an ongoing sense. EMET's "sustained" is adequate but LOGOS's "upheld" better captures the continuous divine support.

**Status:** Resolved in favor of LOGOS. Minor lexical divergence.

---

## 21:10 — "as though we did not exist / as if we were not"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "we-are as-if [we were] not [at all]" | Preserves the Syriac negative existential idiom literally |
| LOGOS | "we are as though we did not exist at all" | Formal expansion of the idiom |
| PNEUMA | "we are as if we never existed at all" | Natural modern equivalent |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The phrase is a characteristic Syriac expression of human insignificance before God. LOGOS preserves the idiom while remaining clear. EMET's bracketed approach is accurate but cumbersome.

**Status:** Resolved in favor of LOGOS. Idiomatic rendering.

---

## 21:14 — "fallen asleep / already died"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "those-who-have-fallen-asleep" | Preserves the Syriac euphemism for death literally |
| LOGOS | "those who have fallen asleep" | Retains the euphemism in formal English |
| PNEUMA | "those who have already died" | Renders functionally for modern clarity |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Retained LOGOS/EMET "fallen asleep." The euphemism is theologically significant in 2 Baruch's resurrection discourse — the dead "sleep" awaiting awakening. PNEUMA's clarification loses this intentional imagery.

**Status:** Resolved in favor of EMET/LOGOS. Theologically significant idiom preserved.

---

## 21:17 — "treasury / treasury of souls"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "the-treasury-[of-souls]" | Brackets "of souls" as implied from context and ch. 23 |
| LOGOS | "the treasury" | Leaves the term unglossed, consistent with source |
| PNEUMA | "the heavenly treasury" | Adds "heavenly" for modern readers' orientation |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS bare "treasury." The full expression "treasury of souls" is explicit in ch. 30 and can be understood from context. EMET's bracket is helpful but potentially anticipatory; PNEUMA's "heavenly" is an addition without textual warrant.

**Status:** Resolved in favor of LOGOS. Contextual sufficiency argument.

---

## 21:22 — "furnace is full"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "your-furnace [is] full" | Literal: the furnace/receptacle awaiting the end |
| LOGOS | "your furnace is full" | Formal equivalent |
| PNEUMA | "Your furnace is full and ready" | Adds "and ready" for dramatic clarity |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The "furnace" here likely refers to the completion of the appointed number of souls (linking to ch. 23's treasury). PNEUMA's addition "and ready" is not in the text.

**Status:** Resolved in favor of LOGOS. Addition removed.

---

## 21:25 — doxological closing

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "Great-is your-strength... great [is] your-glory; great [is] your-beauty, and-great [is] your-grace, and-great [is] your-compassion. Amen, amen." | Preserves the Syriac fivefold doxology with full repetition |
| LOGOS | "For great is your strength, O Lord, and great is your glory; great is your beauty, and great is your grace, and great is your compassion. Amen, amen." | Formal preservation of all five attributes |
| PNEUMA | "Great is your strength, O Lord; great is your glory; great is your beauty; great is your grace; great is your compassion. Amen and amen." | Punctuation varies; "Amen and amen" for natural cadence |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS with PNEUMA's "Amen and amen." The fivefold doxology is a liturgical set piece that should be rendered fully and formally. "Amen and amen" (PNEUMA) has good liturgical precedent and flows more naturally.

**Status:** Resolved as hybrid. Doxological register preserved.

---
